words.gloss: with the man of the land (part 1)

literal: I will not agree, I am not; I will agree, of the hill / fighting male elephant stepped on, broken-branched Vengai tree / hill-tribe women, in their hair to wear, / standing to pluck, blooms, with the man of the land / I will not agree, O friend, but he has united indeed.
translation: I am not one to say 'I will not unite'; I will indeed unite. But how can I say I will not unite with the lord of the land, O friend, where the Vengai tree, its branches crushed by a fighting bull elephant, blooms with flowers that the daughters of the hill-folk can stand and pluck to adorn their hair? He has already united with me.
modern: தோழி! நான் அவனுடன் சேரமாட்டேன் என்று சொல்லவில்லை; சேரவே செய்வேன். சண்டையிடும் ஆண் யானை மிதித்ததால் கிளைகள் உடைந்த வேங்கை மரத்தின் மலர்களை, குறவர் வீட்டுப் பெண்கள் தங்கள் கூந்தலில் சூடுவதற்காக நின்று கொண்டே பறிக்கும்படியாக மலரும் மலைநாட்டை உடைய தலைவனுடன் நான் சேரமாட்டேன் என்று எப்படிச் சொல்வேன்? அவன் ஏற்கனவே என்னோடு மனதால் ஒன்றிவிட்டானே!
explanation: The heroine is speaking to her close friend who is concerned about her secret love affair. She reassures her friend that she is completely committed to the hero and has no intention of refusing him. The imagery of the Vengai tree, whose branch was crushed by a fighting elephant but now bends low enough for the hill-tribe girls to easily pluck its flowers, serves as an uḷḷurai (implied metaphor). It suggests that although the hero is powerful and formidable like the elephant, he has humbled himself to make his love accessible to the heroine. The key words are 'ஒன்றேன்' (I will not unite), 'ஒன்றுவென்' (I will unite), and 'ஒன்றினானே' (he has united indeed), which emphasize the theme of spiritual and physical union.
